blocks.text: Every earlier lesson in this module looked at one piece of MCP in isolation, tool schemas, resource uris, capability negotiation, transports.
This lesson puts all those pieces back together by following a single user message from the moment it is typed to the moment an answer comes back.
Think of this as the interview question where you stop describing parts and instead narrate the whole system, end to end, from memory.
1. The User Types a Message in the Host

blocks.alt: Full journey of one message through host, client, transport, server, and back

blocks.text: Say the user is in Claude Desktop and types, can you check my open GitHub issues and summarize them.
The host application is Claude Desktop itself here, the program the user is actually looking at.
The host is not a passive text box, it already holds the running conversation history and decides when a tool might be needed.
What Counts as Context at This Very First Moment

items: The system prompt the host was configured with.
Every prior message in this conversation, both from the user and the model.
Any resources the user already attached earlier in the chat.
The list of tool schemas the client learned about when it first connected to servers.

blocks.text: Why the Host Matters, Not Just the Model
The model only ever sees what the host chooses to include, the host is the one deciding what counts as context on any given turn.
Two different hosts talking to the same model and the same MCP server can still produce different behavior, because each host assembles context differently.
2. The Host Assembles the Context Window

blocks.alt: The host assembles system prompt, history, and tools into the context window

blocks.text: Before the model sees anything, the host packs all of that into one context window and sends it in.
This is the same context window budget from the earlier lesson on context windows, and tool schemas already eat into it before a single tool is even called.

blocks.text: 3. The Host Hands the Turn to the Model, Then to the Client
The model reads the assembled context and decides it cannot answer from memory alone, it needs the list_issues tool.
The model does not speak MCP itself, it emits a structured intent, call this tool with these arguments, in its own provider specific function calling format.

blocks.title: Translation happens here
blocks.content: The host's MCP client is the piece that turns the model's tool call intent into an actual MCP protocol message. The model never writes JSON-RPC directly.

blocks.text: Until this translation step, nothing MCP specific has happened at all, everything before it was just the host and the model talking.
4. Capability Negotiation Already Happened, Earlier
None of this works if the client and server never met before this message, and by now they already have.
Recall the initialize handshake from the capability negotiation lesson, it ran once, back when the connection first opened, long before this user typed anything.

items: Which protocol version both sides agreed to use.
The full list of tools the server exposes, including list_issues and its schema.
Whether the server also exposes resources or supports sampling.
Any server metadata the client cached for the rest of the session.

blocks.text: Because that handshake already happened, the client already knows this tool exists and already has its schema on hand, no round trip needed just to ask.
Why This Caching Matters for Every Later Message
If negotiation had to repeat on every single message, every user turn would carry the extra cost of rediscovering tools that never changed.
Instead the cached capability list from the initial handshake gets reused for the entire session, this message included.
5. The Client Picks a Transport

blocks.alt: The client picks between stdio and HTTP as the transport

blocks.text: Recall the transports covered earlier, a local server usually talks over stdio, a remote server usually talks over streamable HTTP.
In this example the GitHub MCP server runs as a local process, so the client writes to its stdin and reads from its stdout.
Why the Transport Choice Barely Touches Context
The transport only decides how bytes move, not what they mean, the JSON-RPC message contents are identical whether the pipe is stdio or HTTP.
What does change across transports is latency and how failures show up, both matter for reliability, neither changes what context flows.
6. The Request Crosses the Transport as JSON-RPC

blocks.alt: A request crosses the transport encoded as a JSON-RPC message

blocks.text: The client now writes an actual JSON-RPC 2.0 request onto that stdio pipe.
That id of 42 is what lets the client match whatever response arrives later back to this exact call, even if other calls are in flight.
Reading the Envelope Fields

items: jsonrpc, always the string 2.0, marking the message format.
id, a number or string the client chooses, echoed back untouched in the response.
method, tools/call here, telling the server which kind of request this is.
params, the tool name and its arguments, already shaped to match the tool schema.

blocks.text: 7. The Server Validates Against Its Tool Schema
The server reads the request and, before touching anything real, checks the arguments against the JSON schema it declared for list_issues.
This is the exact schema from the tool schemas lesson, repo must be a string, state must be one of a small enum of values.
If the arguments fail validation, the server sends back an error and nothing outside the server has happened yet.
8. The Tool Executes and Touches the Real World

blocks.alt: A tool executes and touches the real world before returning a result

blocks.text: With valid arguments, the server actually runs the tool function, this is the one step in the whole journey with a real side effect.
Conversation history, system prompt, none of that has any say over what happens inside this step, only the arguments do.
Here the server calls the actual GitHub API, gets back a list of open issues, and holds that data in memory for a moment.
9. The Result Travels Back Across the Transport
The server now wraps whatever it fetched into a JSON-RPC response carrying the same id the request came in with.

blocks.title: Content is a list, not a single blob
blocks.content: A tool result can carry multiple content items, plain text, images, or structured data, the client just reads whatever the server sent back.

blocks.text: Errors Can Come Back on This Same Trip Too
Recall the error responses lesson, a failure partway through execution still comes back as a normal JSON-RPC message, often with isError set to true.
The host treats that failed result as context too, the model gets to see the failure and can decide what to try next.
10. The Client Folds the Result Back Into Context

blocks.alt: A tool result is folded back into the conversation context

blocks.text: That JSON-RPC response lands back at the MCP client, which hands the tool result up to the host.
The host appends it to the conversation as a new tool result turn, sitting right after the model's tool call turn.
This is the precise moment a tool result becomes context, not one step earlier, and not one step later.
11. Resources Enter Context a Different Way

blocks.alt: A resource enters context through a read call rather than a tool call

blocks.text: Contrast this with resources from the resource uris and resource templates lessons, those do not arrive because the model called a tool.
A resource gets pulled in when the host or user attaches it, then the client issues its own resources/read call to fetch the content.
The response looks structurally similar to a tool result, but the host tags it as attached resource content rather than a tool outcome.

blocks.title: Same transport, same server, different entry point
blocks.content: A tool result and a resource read can travel over the exact same connection, what differs is which method triggered them and how the host labels the result.

blocks.text: 12. The Enriched Context Goes Back to the Model
The host reassembles the context window one more time, now including that fresh tool result, and sends it to the model again.
The model reads the new context and writes a plain language summary of the open issues for the user.
If the model decides it needs a second tool call first, the whole loop from step 3 onward simply repeats before any final answer appears.
13. Worked Example, One Full Round Trip
Pull the whole chain together for the one request used throughout this lesson, checking open GitHub issues.

items: User types the request inside the host application.
Host assembles context, system prompt, history, cached tool schemas, latest message.
Model decides list_issues is needed and emits a tool call intent.
MCP client turns that intent into a JSON-RPC tools/call request.
Client writes the request over the stdio transport to the local server.
Server validates the arguments against the tool schema before doing anything.
Server calls the real GitHub API and collects the result.
Server sends a JSON-RPC response back over the same transport, same id.
Client hands the result to the host, which appends it as a tool result turn.
Host resends enriched context to the model, which writes the final summary.

blocks.text: Every earlier lesson maps onto exactly one of these ten steps, that is the whole point of drawing it as one line.
In an interview, naming which lesson each step comes from is often more convincing than naming the steps themselves.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming the model itself sends JSON-RPC, the client is the translator, the model only emits an intent.
Forgetting that capability negotiation already ran, treating every tool call as if the two sides just met for the first time.
Mixing up when a tool result becomes context versus when a resource becomes context, they enter through different calls.
Believing the transport changes the meaning of a message, it only changes how bytes travel, not the JSON-RPC content.
Skipping schema validation in your mental model, believing arguments always reach the tool function untouched.

blocks.text: 15. Practice
Pick any tool from an earlier lesson and narrate its own full round trip the same way, out loud, in under two minutes.

blocks.text: If you can narrate all ten steps without notes, you understand how MCP actually moves context, not just what each piece is called.
Key Takeaway
Context in MCP is not one big blob, it is a sequence of small, well defined entry points, tool schemas at connect time, tool results after a call, resource content on read.
Once you can trace one message through host, client, transport, server, and back, every earlier lesson stops being a separate fact and becomes one step in a single mental model.
